scenes.narration: Tirzepatide is in both Mounjaro and Zepbound, so what's actually different for you?
Short answer: it's the same medicine. Both are tirzepatide, both are made by Eli Lilly, and both are once-weekly injections under the skin.
What's different is the US label. That means who each one is approved for, and the trials behind it. And the devices? That part might surprise you.

Here's the first one, in plain words. In the US, Mounjaro's label is for type 2 diabetes, including lowering heart risk in some adults with it, and Zepbound's label is for weight management and obstructive sleep apnea, in the populations listed.
And stay for the device chapter, because both of these brands come in a form a lot of people haven't heard of.
Picture someone we'll call Dana, 52. She's at the pharmacy counter collecting her Zepbound, and the label on the bag says tirzepatide.
That weekend at dinner, her brother says, 'I'm on Mounjaro. Same thing, right?' And Dana suddenly wonders if one of them has the wrong medicine.
If you've felt that little jolt of confusion, you're not alone. Two brand names for one molecule is genuinely confusing, and asking about it is the smart move.
So let's read the two US labels the way a pharmacist would, section by section, and see exactly where they split.
So who is each one actually approved for?
In every US prescribing label, the first numbered section is Section 1, Indications and Usage. Think of it as the official guest list: the people a medicine is approved to treat.

Mounjaro's Section 1 lists two uses. One: alongside diet and exercise, to improve blood sugar control in people with type 2 diabetes. Two: to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
And it isn't only adults. The FDA has approved Mounjaro's blood sugar use in children aged 10 and older with type 2 diabetes.
Mounjaro's label also has its own warnings section. We'll get to the warnings both labels share in a minute.

scenes.on_screen_text: US Mounjaro: no weight use listed
scenes.narration: Now notice what isn't on Mounjaro's guest list. Its US Section 1 doesn't list weight management.
Zepbound's Section 1 has two uses. Both are alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity.
Use one: to reduce excess body weight and keep it off long term, in adults with obesity, or adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related condition.
Use two: to treat moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.
Zepbound's label also notes that it contains tirzepatide, and that using it together with other tirzepatide products or other GLP-1 medicines isn't recommended.
Which answers Dana's dinner-table moment. She and her brother are on the same molecule, under two different US labels, for different approved uses.
Labels do get updated, so the current Section 1 is always the final word. But a label is only as strong as the trials behind it, and that's where it gets interesting.

scenes.on_screen_text: Where did the labels come from?
scenes.narration: Where did those two guest lists come from?

Mounjaro's blood sugar use rests on the SURPASS trial programme, run in adults with type 2 diabetes. Its heart-risk use comes from SURPASS-CVOT, in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
Take SURPASS-1. Adults with type 2 diabetes managed with diet and exercise alone took tirzepatide or a placebo for 40 weeks.
HbA1c, the roughly three-month blood sugar average, fell by about one point nine to two point one percentage points across the three tirzepatide doses. On placebo, it barely moved.
The children's indication comes from SURPASS-PEDS, a trial in young people with type 2 diabetes, aged 10 to 17.
Zepbound's weight label rests on SURMOUNT. SURMOUNT-1 enrolled 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes.
Over 72 weeks, average weight change on tirzepatide ranged from about 15 to 21 percent, depending on dose. On placebo, it was three point one percent.
And the sleep apnea use? That came from a completely different pair of trials.

SURMOUNT-OSA ran two 52-week trials in adults with obesity and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. One enrolled people not using a breathing machine like CPAP. The other enrolled people who were.
The main measure was breathing interruptions per hour of sleep. In the trial without a machine, they fell by about 25 an hour on tirzepatide, versus about 5 on placebo.
In the trial with a machine, the drop was about 29 an hour on tirzepatide. On placebo, it was about five and a half.
Same molecule in every one of these trials. But very different people, and that matters a lot for what comes next.
So why does Zepbound's side-effect table look so different from Mounjaro's?
Flip to Section 6 of each label and the percentages don't line up. That can feel unsettling, as if one brand is harsher than the other.

But each table comes from its own trial pool. Mounjaro's comes from adults with type 2 diabetes. Zepbound's comes from weight-management trials: one that excluded type 2 diabetes, and one that enrolled only people with it.
Different trial populations, so the tables can't be compared head to head.
Here's a real example: acute pancreatitis, a rare but serious inflammation of the pancreas.
In Mounjaro's diabetes trials, it was reported at zero point two three people per 100 years of exposure. In the comparator groups, zero point one one.
In Zepbound's weight trials, it was zero point one four on tirzepatide, versus zero point one five on placebo.
Same molecule, different numbers. The people, the comparators and the trial designs all differed, so each table is read on its own terms.
Stomach side effects like nausea and diarrhea were the most common in both labels. In the Zepbound label, they happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.
One more from the Zepbound weight trials. Hair loss was reported in five point four percent of people on tirzepatide. On placebo, zero point nine percent.
So the tables differ. But some parts of these two labels are identical, and those are the parts most worth knowing.
What do both labels say in exactly the same way?
Both carry the same boxed warning, the most prominent kind the FDA uses. In rats, tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumors.
It's unknown whether tirzepatide causes these tumors in humans, including a type called medullary thyroid carcinoma.
And both labels say not to use it if you or a family member has had medullary thyroid carcinoma, or if you have Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2.
Both also list warnings for pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, low blood sugar when used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney problems linked to dehydration, and serious allergic reactions.
And both note that tirzepatide may make birth control pills less effective. If you use them, that's a conversation worth having with your prescriber.

scenes.on_screen_text: Trouble breathing, swelling, or severe stomach pain that won't go away: get help right away. 911 US/Canada, 999 UK, 000 Australia.
scenes.narration: If you have trouble breathing, or swelling of your face, lips or throat, call 911 in the US or Canada, 999 in the UK, or 000 in Australia right away. If you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.

scenes.on_screen_text: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
And please don't switch between Mounjaro and Zepbound on your own either. Which brand fits you is a decision for you and your prescriber.
Now, that device I promised you at the start. This is the part of the label you can actually hold in your hand.
So what does each one actually come in?
Device options are printed in two places in each label: Section 3, Dosage Forms and Strengths, and Section 16, How Supplied.
Mounjaro's US label lists four: a single-dose pen, a single-dose vial, a multi-dose vial, and a KwikPen.
Zepbound's US label lists the same four: a single-dose pen, a single-dose vial, a multi-dose vial, and a KwikPen.
That KwikPen is the one many people haven't heard of. It holds four doses and is for one person only, never shared.
So the loop closes like this: in the US, both labels list the same four device options. Your device can change, even when the medicine inside doesn't.
But here's the practical part. Each device has its own Instructions for Use, a separate leaflet with its own steps. Don't assume a pen's steps carry over to a vial or a KwikPen.
For example, the single-dose pen has its own leaflet, with pictured steps for that pen alone.

scenes.on_screen_text: New device? Ask for a walkthrough
scenes.narration: So if your device ever changes, ask your pharmacist or prescriber to walk you through that device's own Instructions for Use.
And if you're watching from outside the US, there's one more twist.
Is it the same story everywhere? Not quite.
In the European Union, for example, Mounjaro's authorisation covers both type 2 diabetes and weight management. So outside the US, check your own country's product information with your prescriber.
So what do you actually do with all of this?
Back to Dana. Nobody handed her the wrong thing. She and her brother take the same molecule, under two US labels, for different approved uses.
And her worry turned into four good questions for her next appointment. Here they are.
One: which label am I on, and for which approved use?
Two: which device is mine, and have I read its own Instructions for Use?
Three: do any of the label's warnings apply to me, like a thyroid history in my family?
Four: should any of my other medicines, including birth control pills, be reviewed?
If this cleared up something that's been nagging you, subscribe. We take one tirzepatide question at a time and answer it from the labels and the trials.

scenes.on_screen_text: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.narration: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.

scenes.narration: How much weight can you lose on tirzepatide, Mounjaro? Here's what the big trial found.
In the SURMOUNT-1 trial, people on the 15 milligram arm lost an average of 20.9 percent of their body weight. That was over 72 weeks.
On placebo, the average loss was 3.1 percent. Everyone in the trial was an adult with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes.
Here's a second number. On that same 15 milligram arm, 57 percent of people lost at least a fifth of their body weight. On placebo, 3 percent did.
But you're the one holding the pen, and you want to know where you might land.
Picture someone like Dana, 48, imagined for this video. A few months in, her scale moved fast, then slowed, and a friend on the same medicine is losing faster.

scenes.on_screen_text: Fat or muscle? Wait for it
scenes.narration: Stick around for the fat-or-muscle chapter, because placebo shows something about that lost weight that's easy to miss.
First, what 'average' really means. Then how much people varied, why diabetes changes things, and the habits experts recommend alongside it.
So who exactly is the 'average' in a trial like this?
Quick note first. Mounjaro and Zepbound are both tirzepatide. In the US, Zepbound is approved for chronic weight management, and Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes.
SURMOUNT-1 randomly assigned 2,539 adults to one of four groups, for 72 weeks.
630 people got the 5 milligram arm. 636 got 10 milligrams. 630 got 15 milligrams. And 643 got placebo.
Those are trial arms, not a plan for you. Your prescriber decides yours.
Here's a detail that changes how you read the results. Every group, placebo included, also got regular lifestyle counselling, with a reduced-calorie eating plan and physical activity goals.
So the placebo group wasn't doing nothing. Their 3.1 percent loss is roughly what counselling plus a dummy injection achieved here.
And the main numbers count everyone who started, including people who stopped their injections early. That's a stricter way to report results, and closer to real life.
So, counting everyone, here's each arm at 72 weeks. On the 5 milligram arm, the average loss was 15 percent.
On the 10 milligram arm, the average loss was 19.5 percent.
On the 15 milligram arm, it was 20.9 percent. And on placebo, 3.1 percent.
To make that concrete: for someone starting at 100 kilograms, about 220 pounds, a 20.9 percent loss would be about 21 kilograms. That's roughly 46 pounds. Just arithmetic, not a prediction.
But an average is just one dot on a chart, and real people are scattered around it. So how far apart were they?
If the average on the top arm was about a fifth, did everyone lose about a fifth?
No. The paper reports what share of people crossed each line, and the spread is wide.
Start with a loss of at least 5 percent. On the tirzepatide arms, 85 to 91 percent of people reached it, depending on the arm. On placebo, 35 percent did.
Flip that around. On the 15 milligram arm, roughly 1 in 10 people didn't reach a 5 percent loss, even after 72 weeks.
Next line: a loss of at least 15 percent. That was about 48 percent of people on the 5 milligram arm, about 67 percent on 10, and about 71 percent on 15. On placebo, fewer than 1 in 10.
And a loss of at least 20 percent: about 30 percent of people on 5 milligrams, 50 percent on 10, and 57 percent on 15. On placebo, 3 percent.
Now picture ten people from the 15 milligram arm around one table. Five or six lost a fifth or more. One didn't reach 5 percent. The rest landed in between.
If your loss is slower than someone else's, that's not a willpower verdict. People on the exact same arm, with the same counselling, had very different results.
This trial wasn't built to predict who loses what, so these shares describe groups, not your personal future.
Back to Dana and her faster friend. Same medicine, different bodies. The trial shows gaps like that between people on the same arm. It's not proof Dana is doing anything wrong.
But one group lost noticeably less on average, and it got its own trial.
So does having type 2 diabetes change how much weight people lose on tirzepatide?
That was tested in SURMOUNT-2. It's a separate trial with different people, so it's not a head-to-head with SURMOUNT-1.
It enrolled 938 adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, for 72 weeks. 312 got the 10 milligram arm, 311 got 15 milligrams, and 315 got placebo.
Counting everyone who started, the average loss on the 10 milligram arm was 12.8 percent.
On the 15 milligram arm, it was 14.7 percent. On placebo, 3.2 percent.
And 79 to 83 percent of people on the tirzepatide arms lost at least 5 percent of their weight, compared with 32 percent on placebo.
So people with type 2 diabetes tend to lose less on average, across weight-loss trials in general. Why? The reasons aren't fully established.

scenes.on_screen_text: Ask what it means for you
scenes.narration: So we won't guess. If you have type 2 diabetes, ask your prescriber what this trial means for you, because your full picture matters more than any average.
Now, the chapter I promised at the start. When the scale drops by a fifth, what exactly is leaving the body?
How much of the weight lost on tirzepatide was fat, and how much was lean mass?
Inside SURMOUNT-1, 160 people had DXA scans. That's a low-dose X-ray scan that separates fat from lean tissue. They were scanned at the start and at week 72.
The three tirzepatide doses were pooled together and compared with placebo.
On tirzepatide, body weight fell by 21.3 percent in this group.
Fat mass fell by about a third. That's 33.9 percent of the fat people started with.
Lean mass fell too. That drop was 10.9 percent.
Put those together, and about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat. About a quarter was lean mass.
Now here's the part that's easy to miss. People on placebo lost less, 5.3 percent of body weight. But their split was the same. About three-quarters fat, about a quarter lean.
So that ratio isn't unique to tirzepatide. In this study, it's what weight loss looked like in both groups.
One more thing. Lean mass isn't pure muscle. It also includes water, organs and other tissue that isn't fat.
And this body-scan study didn't directly measure strength or physical performance. So it can't tell us whether that lean loss is harmful or harmless. Anyone who's certain is going past the data.

scenes.on_screen_text: Give muscle a reason to stay
scenes.narration: For Dana, that's useful, not scary. The goal isn't to fear lean loss. It's to give her muscles good reasons to stay. And that's where habits come in.
So what can you actually do to protect muscle while you lose weight?
An honesty check first. SURMOUNT-1 didn't test a protein target or strength training. These are general recommendations from expert groups, not proven tirzepatide results.
A 2025 joint advisory on nutrition alongside GLP-1 medicines emphasizes getting enough protein and doing strength training.
Habit one: include a protein source at each meal, unless your clinician has told you to limit protein, for example because of kidney disease.
When your appetite is smaller, eating the protein part of your plate first is one simple way to keep it from getting crowded out.
Habit two: muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days a week, working all the major muscle groups. That's the World Health Organization's recommendation for adults.

Start gently. Sit-to-stands from a chair, wall push-ups or resistance bands all count, and the WHO says some activity is better than none. If you have a heart, joint or other condition, check with your clinician first.
Picture Dana. Two mornings a week, ten minutes of chair stands and band rows. Eggs or yogurt at breakfast. Not heroic. Just repeatable.
But the most useful habit might not happen at home at all. It happens in a short conversation with your prescriber.
So what's worth asking the person who prescribes it?
Start with side effects. In SURMOUNT-1, the most common were stomach-related, like nausea, diarrhea and constipation. They happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time.
In SURMOUNT-1, 2.6 percent of people on placebo stopped because of side effects. On the tirzepatide arms, it was 4.3 to 7.1 percent.

scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain? Get help right away
scenes.narration: If you get severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Talk to your prescriber.
Here are five questions worth bringing. One: what would a good result look like for me, beyond the scale? Two: does type 2 diabetes, or anything else I have, change what to expect?
Three: how much protein is right for me? Four: which strength activities are safe for me to start? Five: which side effects should I call you about?
Because weight is one health measure among many. Blood pressure, blood sugar, how you move and how you feel all count too.

scenes.on_screen_text: Is it right for you? Ask
scenes.narration: Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

So, how much weight can you lose on tirzepatide? In SURMOUNT-1, in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, average losses ran from 15 percent to 20.9 percent across the arms over 72 weeks. Placebo: 3.1 percent.

People varied widely. In a separate trial of adults with type 2 diabetes, average losses were smaller. And in a body-scan study of 160 SURMOUNT-1 participants, about a quarter of the weight lost was lean mass, on tirzepatide and placebo alike.
Protein at each meal and strength work at least twice a week are the habits experts recommend alongside it.
If you'd like more trial results explained this plainly, including what months 2 to 6 on tirzepatide can look like, subscribe.
Dana's scale will do what scales do. But she knows what the trials really showed, and what to ask. There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.

scenes.on_screen_text: Tirzepatide: what do months 2–6 look like?
scenes.narration: You're past your first month on tirzepatide, so what do months two to six look like?
Short answer: in the Zepbound label's trials, stomach side effects happened mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time.
And in the main weight trial, average weight kept going down over months, not weeks, then levelled off later in the 72-week trial.
Here's one number up front. In the Zepbound weight-management trials, nausea was reported by 25 to 29 percent of people on tirzepatide, depending on dose, versus 8 percent on placebo.
Flip that around. Roughly 7 in 10 people on tirzepatide in those trials didn't report nausea at all.
Picture Dana, 47. She's imaginary, but her questions might sound familiar.
She's five weeks in. The first-month jitters have faded, but fresh questions keep arriving. Will the quiet around food last? Will the nausea come back? Why is the scale slower some weeks?
If you feel that same mix of hope and worry, you're not alone. It's a very human place to be.

scenes.on_screen_text: Hair: a gap between women and men
scenes.narration: And stay for the hair chapter. There's a gap between women and men that rarely gets mentioned.
One honest note first. The US labels don't give a month-by-month calendar. So we'll go by the evidence: the Zepbound and Mounjaro labels and the big SURMOUNT-1 trial.

scenes.on_screen_text: Will the quiet around food last?
scenes.narration: First question: will the quiet around food last?
You might call it food noise: that running chatter about the next snack. It's a term viewers use, not one the label uses.

Here's what the Zepbound label does say. GLP-1 is a natural regulator of appetite and calorie intake. Receptors for both GIP and GLP-1 are found in brain areas involved in appetite, and animal studies show tirzepatide reaches and activates those areas.
The label also says tirzepatide slows how fast the stomach empties. That delay is largest after the first dose and lessens over time, so it's one measured effect, not the whole story of appetite.
Here's the honest part. Nothing in the label promises that food noise stays quiet for good.
Some weeks, Dana's appetite feels turned way down. Other weeks, on a stressful day, the old cravings knock again.
That isn't a willpower failure. It's a body and a brain, not a machine, and appetite can vary from week to week.
Having a plan for the louder weeks helps, and we'll build one in the last chapter. First, the stomach.
Does the nausea come back when the dose goes up?
Here's what the label found. In the trials, nausea, diarrhea and vomiting happened mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time.
The SURMOUNT-1 paper said something similar. The most common side effects were stomach-related, mostly mild to moderate, and they happened primarily during dose escalation.
Here's why that matters for these months. Months two to six often include dose increases, on whatever schedule your prescriber sets.

scenes.on_screen_text: Queasy after a step up? Tell them
scenes.narration: So a queasy few days after a step up fits the pattern the trials saw. It doesn't automatically mean something's wrong, but it's worth mentioning to your prescriber.
How many people stopped because of side effects? In SURMOUNT-1, on tirzepatide, the low end was four point three percent. The high end was seven point one percent, depending on dose.
On placebo, it was two point six percent, over the same 72 weeks. So more than 9 in 10 people on tirzepatide didn't stop because of side effects.
One more label point. Kidney problems have been reported, mostly in people who got dehydrated from nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.
So sip fluids through a rough patch, and tell your prescriber if you can't keep fluids down.

scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain that won't go away? Get help right away
scenes.narration: One sign is never wait-and-see. If you have severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, get medical help right away.
In an emergency, call nine one one in the US or Canada, nine nine nine in the UK, or triple zero in Australia.

scenes.on_screen_text: Don't stop or change it on your own
scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
Next, the scale. Why does it race some weeks and barely budge in others? The trial curve explains that better than any single weigh-in.

scenes.on_screen_text: What does the curve look like?
scenes.narration: So what does weight change actually look like across months?

scenes.on_screen_text: SURMOUNT-1: 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight + a weight-related condition, without diabetes
scenes.narration: SURMOUNT-1 enrolled 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes.
They took tirzepatide or placebo for 72 weeks, alongside a lifestyle program.
Picture the tirzepatide average as a line on a chart. It didn't drop off a cliff in month one.

scenes.on_screen_text: Down over months, then levels off
scenes.narration: It kept going down over months, not weeks, then levelled off later in the 72-week trial.
The placebo line moved far less. At week 72, the placebo group's average weight was three point one percent lower.

scenes.on_screen_text: SURMOUNT-1, week 72: average weight 15–20.9% lower on tirzepatide vs 3.1% on placebo
scenes.narration: On tirzepatide, across the three doses, average weight at week 72 was 15 to almost 21 percent lower, in that same trial population.
But averages aren't predictions. At week 72, 85 to 91 percent of people on tirzepatide had lost at least 5 percent of their body weight, versus 35 percent on placebo.
That also means a smaller group on tirzepatide didn't reach even that 5 percent mark. Bodies respond differently.
For Dana, a slow week in month three isn't a verdict. An average line is smooth. A real person's scale is jagged, with water and meals in the mix.
If your line flattens, we have separate videos on plateaus and on how long tirzepatide takes to work.
Next, the chapter I promised. A few months in, some people notice more hair in the brush, and the gap between women and men is striking.
Is extra hair shedding normal on tirzepatide?

scenes.on_screen_text: That jolt of worry is real
scenes.narration: Picture Dana in the shower, a few months in, seeing more strands than usual. That jolt of worry is real, and it's okay to feel it.
In the Zepbound weight-management trials, hair loss was reported by five point four percent of people on tirzepatide.
On placebo, it was zero point nine percent.
Here's the gap. Among women on tirzepatide, it was seven point one percent.
Among men on tirzepatide, it was zero point five percent.

scenes.on_screen_text: May be linked to the weight loss itself
scenes.narration: Why? The label doesn't settle it. One possibility is that shedding like this may be linked to the weight loss itself.

scenes.on_screen_text: Shedding: a few months after a trigger
scenes.narration: The American Academy of Dermatology lists losing 20 pounds or more as one trigger for excess shedding. Most people notice it a few months after the trigger.

scenes.on_screen_text: Tends to stop as body readjusts
scenes.narration: It also says this kind of shedding tends to stop as the body readjusts.

scenes.on_screen_text: Patchy or lasting? See a doctor
scenes.narration: But see a doctor if hair comes out in patches, or if the shedding doesn't settle. Those are worth a proper look.
Next, a label note that lands right in this window. It only matters if you use one kind of birth control.
Do you use an oral birth control pill? This chapter is for you.
Both the Mounjaro and Zepbound labels say tirzepatide may make oral hormonal birth control less effective.
The labels name two windows: the 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide, and the 4 weeks after each dose increase.

scenes.on_screen_text: Can come up more than once
scenes.narration: Because months two to six often include dose increases, this note can come up more than once.

scenes.on_screen_text: Ask about non-oral or backup options
scenes.narration: For those weeks, the labels suggest switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method like condoms. Ask your prescriber which backup option fits you.
To be clear, this note is about oral hormonal birth control. That's the method the labels name.
One more body change, and it's the one you can actually see on your skin.
What about a red or itchy patch where you inject?
In the Zepbound weight-management trials, injection-site reactions were reported by 6 to 8 percent of people on tirzepatide, depending on dose, versus about 2 percent on placebo.
So it happens, but in a small share of people.
The Mounjaro Instructions for Use say to change your injection site each week. You can use the same body area, just a different spot within it.

scenes.on_screen_text: Face swelling or trouble breathing? Get help right away
scenes.narration: If you notice swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing, get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
A mild red patch is a fair question for your prescriber or pharmacist.
So that's what tends to change. Next, what actually helps you through it.
So what can make months two to six easier?
Start with the label. Zepbound is meant to be used alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. The medicine is one part of the plan.
A helpful habit: build meals around protein, which may help you hold on to muscle while you lose weight. If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor before you increase protein.
Gentle strength training, started slowly, can help too. If you have a heart, joint or other health condition, clear it with your clinician first.
On queasy weeks, smaller meals, eating slowly and stopping when you're full may make things easier.

scenes.on_screen_text: On insulin or a sulfonylurea? Ask
scenes.narration: One more safety note. If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, your risk of low blood sugar may be higher. Ask your prescriber what signs to watch for.
Here are four questions worth bringing to your next appointment.
What should I do on a rough nausea week? And if I use oral birth control, what backup should I use around dose increases?
Is my hair shedding worth checking? And is this injection-site reaction okay, or should someone look at it?
Back to Dana. Five weeks in, she wanted to know what's next. Here's what the evidence gives her.

In the Zepbound label's trials, stomach side effects happened mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time. In SURMOUNT-1, average weight on tirzepatide kept falling over months, then levelled off later in the 72 weeks.

scenes.on_screen_text: Hair loss on tirzepatide: more common in women
scenes.narration: In the Zepbound weight-management trials, hair loss was more common on tirzepatide than on placebo, and among people on tirzepatide, more common in women than in men.
If you use oral birth control, ask about backup for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. And change your injection spot each week.
Appetite may get louder some weeks. That's a body, not a failure, and protein plus gentle strength work can support you along the way.
This is part of our series on your first months with tirzepatide. Subscribe, and the next part will find you.

scenes.on_screen_text: Not personal advice: ask your prescriber
scenes.narration: Not personal advice. Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine, so talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

scenes.narration: Redness, itching, bruising or pain where you inject tirzepatide is a known side effect. In the trials it was reported by six to eight percent of people on it. And a small spot that stays put and fades is the ordinary pattern.
But that's not much comfort at seven in the morning. You're getting dressed the day after your shot, and you spot it: a pink patch, a little warm, maybe a bit itchy.
Your brain goes straight to the worst questions. Is this an allergy? Did I do something wrong? Should I be worried?
If that's you, you're not alone, and it's a fair thing to wonder. So let's answer it with the actual label, not a forum thread.
In the next few minutes, you'll get the real numbers for every dose arm against placebo, what a lump or a bruise usually means, and what the Instructions for Use say about where to inject.
And stay for the end, because there's one simple difference that separates 'leave it alone' from 'call today'. It's the most useful thing in this video.

scenes.on_screen_text: A clue in the placebo group
scenes.narration: Plus, there's a quiet clue hiding in the placebo group. It tells you something surprising about where these reactions come from.
First, how common is this, really?
The Zepbound prescribing information, revised in August twenty twenty-six, has a side-effect table from its placebo-controlled weight-management trials in adults with obesity or overweight.

The biggest of those trials, SURMOUNT-1, randomly assigned two thousand five hundred thirty-nine adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related health problem, and without diabetes, to one of three tirzepatide doses or placebo, for seventy-two weeks. It was double-blind, so nobody knew which they had. The label's table pools it with a second trial in adults with type 2 diabetes.
On placebo, two percent reported an injection site reaction.
On the five-milligram tirzepatide arm, it was six percent.
On ten milligrams, eight percent. And on fifteen milligrams, eight percent too.

Eight percent sounds abstract, so picture a room of twenty-five people on the ten or fifteen milligram dose. About two of them would notice something at the injection site. The other twenty-three wouldn't.
Notice something? The lowest dose came in at six percent, but going from ten to fifteen milligrams didn't add anything. Both sat at eight.
So in this table, a higher dose didn't simply keep adding reactions. It's a small gap, so don't read too much into it either way.
What counts as a reaction? The label groups several terms under one heading, including bruising, redness, itching, pain and rash at the injection site.
And here's something you might not expect. Injection site reactions made the label's list of most common side effects, right alongside nausea, diarrhea and constipation.
In other words, the label treats this as a known possibility, not a mystery. That alone takes some of the fear out of a pink patch.
So why does your skin react at all? Here's where that placebo clue comes in.
In these trials, the placebo group got injections too, on the same weekly schedule. That's how you keep a trial blind: everyone goes through the same routine.
So the placebo group had the needle and the routine, but not the medicine. And only two percent of them reported a reaction.
Add tirzepatide, and it rose to six to eight percent. That hints the medicine itself plays a part, not just the needle going in.

scenes.on_screen_text: Built on GIP + a fatty chain
scenes.narration: So what is that medicine, physically? The label says tirzepatide is built on the sequence of GIP, one of your own gut hormones, with a fatty chain attached. That fatty chain helps it latch onto a protein in your blood, so it lasts all week.
Put simply, an injection site reaction is your skin responding right where that medicine was placed under it.

scenes.on_screen_text: A link, not a full explanation
scenes.narration: The label does note one link: in its weight trials, reactions were more common in people whose bodies made antibodies to tirzepatide. That's a link, not a full explanation, and you can't tell from a pink patch whether it applies to you. So be wary of anyone online who claims to know exactly why yours happened.
But knowing it's common is only half the story. The next question is the one that really gets people: what about a lump?
Let's talk about the small lump, and the bruise.
Here's our own plain-language take, not a quote from the label. A small, firm bump, or a little bruise, can happen after an injection under the skin.
A needle can nick a tiny blood vessel on the way in, and that can leave a small bruise, much like a blood test sometimes does.
What usually reassures people is the pattern. An ordinary local reaction tends to stay small, stay in that one spot, and fade over the following days.
So, the calm signs: it's small. It stays put. It isn't getting worse. And you otherwise feel like yourself.
If yours fits that picture, it matches the ordinary pattern. If it doesn't, we'll get to exactly what to do in a moment.
And if you've felt embarrassed asking about something this small, don't be. Pharmacists and nurses are there for exactly this kind of question.
Which brings us to a question we see a lot: does where you inject matter?
Here we'll stick strictly to the Instructions for Use, the official step-by-step guide that comes with the pen.
The Instructions list three areas: your stomach area, at least two inches from your belly button; the front of your thighs; and the back of your upper arm.
For the upper arm, the Instructions say another person should give you the injection.
Then comes the part people skip. The Instructions say to change, or rotate, your injection site each week.
You can use the same body area, but they say to choose a different injection site within that area.
In plain words: same neighborhood, different house each week.
The Instructions don't promise that rotating prevents reactions, so we won't either. But it's what the official guide asks for, and it's easy to do.
If you're unsure about any step, ask your pharmacist or prescriber to walk you through the Instructions in person.
Now, here's where it gets more serious, and this is the worry behind the whole question: could that pink patch be an allergy?
Let's separate two things that often get blurred together.

scenes.on_screen_text: At the spot vs beyond it
scenes.narration: A local reaction happens at the spot. An allergic reaction, which the label calls a hypersensitivity reaction, can go beyond that spot.
In the label's weight-management trials, hypersensitivity reactions were reported in about five percent of people on tirzepatide, versus about three percent on placebo.
That's a broad group of allergy-type reactions, and placebo had some too. The label also notes that serious ones, including anaphylaxis and a type of swelling called angioedema, have been reported.
Those are the ones worth knowing by sight.

The Medication Guide lists signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat; problems breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; and a very rapid heartbeat.

scenes.on_screen_text: Stop using it and get medical help right away
scenes.narration: If any of those happen, the Medication Guide says to stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away. Call your local emergency number or go to emergency care.
Notice the difference. A slightly itchy pink patch on your stomach is one thing. Swelling of your lips, or trouble breathing, is a completely different situation.

scenes.on_screen_text: Not an emergency? Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own
scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. If you think you've had any allergic reaction, even a mild one, talk to your prescriber so they can decide with you.
Which brings us back to the promise from the start: the one difference that separates 'leave it alone' from 'call today'.
Here it is. A normal reaction stays small and settles. A reaction worth a call spreads, gets worse, or comes with feeling unwell.
These next signs are our own safety lines, built from that idea, not a quote from the label.
Call your prescriber if the redness is spreading, if the area feels hot, if there's pus, if you get a fever, or if the reaction keeps getting worse instead of better.

scenes.on_screen_text: Local urgent care or emergency number
scenes.narration: If you can't reach your prescriber and you're worried, contact your local urgent care or emergency number. You never need permission to get checked.
Picture it as two columns. On the left: small, in one spot, fading. On the right: spreading, hot, oozing, fever, or worsening. Left, keep an eye on it. Right, pick up the phone.
And if you're not sure which column you're in, that's a reason to call, not a reason to wait.
If that was the answer you came for, subscribe. We take one practical tirzepatide question at a time and answer it straight from the label and the trials.
Let's pull it all together.
Back to you, standing there with that pink patch the morning after your shot. Here's what you now know.
In the label's weight trials, six to eight percent of people on tirzepatide reported injection site reactions, depending on the dose arm, versus two percent on placebo.
Small, local, not getting worse, and you feel fine? That matches the ordinary pattern.
The Instructions for Use list your stomach area, your thighs and the back of the upper arm, and they say to rotate your site each week.

Spreading redness, heat, pus, fever or worsening means calling your prescriber. Signs of a serious allergic reaction, like swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing, mean what the Medication Guide says: stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away.

scenes.on_screen_text: Drinking fluids helps reduce dehydration risk
scenes.narration: One more thing while we're here. Stomach side effects like nausea, diarrhea and vomiting are among the most common. The Medication Guide says they can cause a loss of fluids, which may cause kidney problems, and that drinking fluids helps reduce your chance of dehydration.

scenes.on_screen_text: Severe or won't go away? Tell them
scenes.narration: If stomach symptoms are severe or won't go away, tell your prescriber.
A pink patch can feel like a big deal when it's on your own body. Now you know how to read it calmly, and when to ask for help.

scenes.on_screen_text: Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
